prompt: Explain a complex scientific concept (like quantum entanglement) using only the vocabulary of a 17th-century pirate.

chatgpt.html:
Aye aye, matey! Gather ‘round and lend me yer ears, for I be about to spin ye a yarn most strange—of ghostly bonds and devilish trickery that’d confound even the saltiest sea dog. I speak o’ a sorcery the landlubbers call quantum entanglement. But fret not, I’ll chart ye through it with words fit for a scallywag.

Now, picture this: ye’ve got two cannonballs, aye, forged from the same accursed iron, and cursed they be with a spell so queer that whatever happens to one, the other feels it too—no matter how far across the seven seas she sails. Blast one off the port side o’ yer ship, and t’other, leagues away off the starboard bow of another vessel,’ll shudder just the same, at the very same moment! Aye, as if Neptune himself were pullin’ the strings.

These cannonballs, once touched by the same magic, become entangled, like twin souls bound by fate. Ye spin one starboard, and the other, though far as the moon, spins port. No signal be sent, no whisper on the wind—just instant knowin’, faster than any ship or albatross could carry.

The King’s scholars say this be no illusion, but the way the world truly works beneath the veil. Aye, ‘tis a realm not of wood and sail, but of mysteries where certainty be as slippery as an eel in a barrel o’ rum.

So mark me words, lads: in the strange and wondrous world below the decks of reality, things be tied together in ways no compass can chart and no map can show. That’s the tale of entanglement, and if it don’t make yer brain feel like a kraken’s knotted beard, then ye ain’t been listenin’.

Now pass the grog—I need it after meddling with such cursed knowledge! Yarrr! 🏴‍☠️

plain.html:

Imagine, if ye will, two magical coins forged by the devil himself, aye. Once these two coins be touched by this dark magic, they forever hold a bond stronger than the chains of Davy Jones’ locker. Even if ye take one o' these coins and sail to the farthest seas, leavin' the other on shores unknown, what happens to one shall be known to the other in the blink of an eye, faster than the swiftest ship or wind could carry the news!

If ye flip one o' the coins, and it shows heads, the other will instantly show tails, no matter how far apart they be—like they be whisperin' secrets across the very ether o' the world. ‘Tis as if the pair be sharin' a hidden code, aye, known only to them. And yet, no earthly spy, no matter how cunning, can crack their silent covenant.

Some say ‘tis but sorcery, and others say ‘tis the true nature o’ the universe, tangled in mysteries greater than even the Kraken itself. But mark me words: these coins don’t talk across the waves like yer shipmates shout orders. Nay! 'Tis a deeper connection, one beyond sight and sound, like they be of one soul, split in twain.

So, matey, next ye hear whispers of “quantum entanglement,” know ye now the tale o' the devil’s coins, bound by fate and magic unbreakable, no matter how far apart the tides may carry 'em. Yarrr!

plain.html:
Arrr, picture two tiny motes born of one strange joining, then carried to opposite ends of the sea.

Each captain may test his mote with a chosen question. The answer be chance; yet when both captains ask the same question, their answers bear a sure kinship. Ask different questions, and the answers follow a stranger rule—one no pair of secret orders, writ beforehand for each mote, can explain.

Yet no shout, raven, nor command flies from one mote to the other. Neither captain can choose his answer or send tidings by it. The two motes simply share one fate, though far apart.

That be the strange joining: entanglement.

instruction.html:
Arrr, picture two wee motes born of one strange bargain. Sail ’em to far shores, and ask each the same sort of question. Their answers be joined: learn one, and ye can tell what answer the other shall give.

Yet ’tis no pair of secret notes penned beforehand. Ask different questions, and the answers show a bond no hidden captain’s plan can account for. Still, no parrot, cannon, nor swift ship carries a message between the shores; neither mote can send news faster than light.

That far-reaching bond, matey, be entanglement.

plain.html:
Aye, matey. Fancy two specks of dust born of one spark. Carry one to Port Royal and t’other clear round the world. Peer at each through a spyglass, and ye’ll spy either a sun or a moon.

Now, ye can twist yer glass this way or that. Set both glasses the same way, and both crews spy the same mark, though neither crew can tell beforehand which mark it’ll be.

“Arr,” says ye, “the marks were fixed afore we sailed!” But twist the glasses to sundry angles and tally what both crews see, voyage after voyage. No set of orders sealed afore they parted can account for all those tallies.

And there’s the rub: ye can’t make yer speck show a sun to warn yer mate of a man-o’-war. Each crew sees what it sees, and the wonder only comes to light when they meet again and lay their logs side by side.

instruction.html:
Arr, take two bewitched pieces of eight. Keep one aboard, and send t’other with a ship bound for the Indies. When each captain sets his coin spinning and claps a hand upon it, neither can tell beforehand which face he’ll find. Yet if both captains use the selfsame turn of the wrist, one finds a king and t’other finds a cross. Every blessed time.

“Why,” says the boatswain, “the faces were settled afore the ships parted!”

A shrewd guess, matey. But let each captain choose among several turns of the wrist, and keep a tally of which turns they used and which faces they found. When the ships meet again, their tallies show a trick no set of answers tucked into the coins at parting could have pulled off.

And there’s no sending word by it, neither. Ye can’t bid yer coin come up king to say “Make sail!” All ye see aboard yer own ship is a jumble of kings and crosses. The marvel’s in how the two tallies fit together, and for that ye’ll have to wait till the other ship comes home.

plain.html:
Arrr, matey, picture a wizard’s mint that strikes two silver pennies at a blow. Keep one aboard thy sloop; send its fellow o’er the sea to Port Royal.

Each captain hath a choice: lay his penny upon the compass card and give it a rap from whatever quarter he pleaseth. Each rap yields a head or a tail, and neither captain can foretell which. Yet whenever both rap from the same quarter, one gets a head and t’other a tail, sure as the tide.

“Bah!” says the bosun. “Each penny sailed with its orders writ for every quarter!”

There’s the marvel, lad. Let each captain choose his quarter afresh for every pair. When the ships meet again, lay their logs side by side. For sundry quarters their tallies agree more often than any such secret orders could contrive.

Canst thou send word o’er the sea by this trick? Nay. Thou canst choose thy quarter, but not thy head or tail. To either captain alone, his tally looks like naught but luck. The wonder lies betwixt the two, and takes both logs to spy.

instruction.html:
Hearken, shipmate. A brace o’ silver pieces comes from a queer mint. Ye take one east to the Indies; I take t’other west to Jamaica. At noon we each spin our piece upon a chart. If our charts lie the same way, then whenever ye get the king’s head, I get his arms, and whenever ye get his arms, I get his head. Yet neither of us can tell, ere his own piece falls, which face he’ll see.

“Aye,” says ye, “the rogue at the mint settled all that afore we sailed.”

Now comes the rub. We have a whole chest o’ such pairs. At each trial ye may turn yer chart to a fresh bearing, and I may do likewise. On our return we lay our logs side by side and reckon how often our pieces fell alike at each pair o’ bearings. No table of answers the rogue might have graven on the silver afore we sailed could yield the whole of that reckoning.

Mark ye, ’tis no way to send word. Ye cannot choose to cast the king’s head and thereby bid me make sail. My log alone reads like so many casts o’ the dice. The wonder lies in what the two logs tell together.

plain.html:
The Tale of the Twin Doubloons

Arrr, gather round, ye scallywags, and I'll spin ye a yarn about the strangest sorcery on the seven seas: the Bewitched Doubloons.

The Forging

Picture two doubloons, forged in a single flash o' hellfire so that their fates be bound together like two men chained to the same anchor. Ye send one with Captain Blackwater to the farthest edge o' the Spanish Main, and the other stays with ye in Tortuga.

The Curse o' the Spinning

Here be the queer part, mateys. Till a man claps eyes on his coin, it be neither heads nor tails. It spins in a ghostly blur, bein' both at once. Not hidden, mind ye. Truly undecided, like a ship in fog that's not yet chosen a harbor.

The Moment o' Lookin'

When ye peek at yer doubloon, it settles. Say it lands heads. At that very instant, Blackwater's coin, a thousand leagues off, lands tails. Every time! Ye'll never find the pair agreein' when they ought to disagree.

"'Tis a Trick!" cry the doubters

Some old sea-dogs scoff: "The coins were marked at the forge, ye fools! Heads and tails were settled from the start, like cards stowed up a sleeve."

But a clever navigator devised a cunning wager. Instead o' lookin' at the coins the same way each time, ye each peek from different angles, as if tiltin' yer spyglass. If the coins were merely marked at the forge, the matchin' could only go so far. Yet when the crews tallied their ledgers, the coins matched more than any hidden marks could explain. The doubters were left speechless, and the sorcery be real.

Now Mind This, Ye Landlubbers

Ye cannot use these coins to send secret messages faster than a gale! When ye look at yer coin, ye get heads or tails by pure chance, like a toss o' the dice. Blackwater likewise sees only chance. 'Tis only when ye meet in port and compare yer ledgers that ye find the two tallies mirror each other perfectly. No message sails between ye. Only the bond be revealed.

The Moral o' the Tale

The sea o' nature be stranger than any kraken. Two things once bound together can share a single fate, no matter how many leagues divide 'em, and no man can say the outcome till he looks.

Now fetch me rum!

Translation for the landlubbers
  • Bewitched doubloons = entangled particles
  • Spinning blur = superposition
  • Lookin' = measurement
  • Marked at the forge = hidden variables
  • The navigator's wager = Bell's theorem and its experimental tests
  • No messages = the no-communication theorem

instruction.html:
The Tale of the Twin Doubloons

Gather round, ye scurvy lot, and I'll spin ye a yarn about the strangest witchcraft ever to curse the deep.

Picture two doubloons, forged together in a sea-witch's cauldron under a black moon. Ye take one and sail to Tortuga. Yer shipmate takes the other and sails to the farthest edge o' the world, past where the maps turn to sea serpents.

Now here's the devilry of it. Neither coin be heads or tails while it lies in yer pouch. Not hidden, mind ye, but truly neither, like a squall that ain't yet decided where to strike. The coin be both and neither, till a man claps eyes on it.

The moment ye look at yer coin, it settles. Say it lands heads. Faster than a cannon's flash, ye know yer mate's coin has fallen tails, though he's a thousand leagues off and hasn't looked at all. Every time, the two agree in their opposition, as if bound by a cursed oath.

"But Cap'n, 'tis only sealed orders!"

Aye, that's what any sensible sailor says. "The coins were tails and heads from the start, like two crewmen carrying sealed orders. Ye just didn't know which." A fair thought!

But clever navigators put it to the test. They didn't just look at the coins one way. They looked from different angles, tilting the lantern this way and that. If the coins had carried sealed orders, the crew's tallies could only agree so often. Yet the tallies agreed more than any sealed orders could explain. The old reckoning fails. The coins truly share one fate, and no secret was written beforehand.

"Then send me word faster than a ship!"

Ha! The witch be cleverer than that, ye greedy dog. When ye look at yer coin, it falls heads or tails by pure chance, and ye can't command which. Yer mate sees only a random scattering, same as ye. Only when ye later sail together and compare yer logs do ye see the match. So no message crosses the waves faster than a ship. The magic be in the bond, not in the bearing of tidings.

The Moral o' the Tale

The sea holds two truths, and both hold fast:

  1. Things once bound can share a single fate, however far the tides carry them apart.
  2. Before ye look, the fate be truly unsettled, not merely unknown to ye.

Even the wisest captains of the age, learned men who'd charted every star, called it "spooky doings at a distance." And aye, 'tis spooky. But the sea don't care what suits a man's sense, and every test o' the thing proves the witch's coins be real.

Now fetch me rum. All this talk o' fate has given me a thirst.

plain.html:
The Tale of the Two Cursed Doubloons

As told by Cap'n Ezekiel Blackwater, aboard the sloop Merry Widow*, Anno Domini 1687*

Gather 'round, ye scurvy lubbers, and belay that rumbullion a moment. I'll spin ye a yarn stranger than any sea-serpent off the Spanish Main.

The Matched Pair

There be a sorcerer's trick whereby two doubloons are struck together in the same cursed forge, so that their fates be bound, one to the other, like two rogues sworn to the same articles.

Now mark me: ye seal one doubloon in a chest and send it to Tortuga. The other ye stow in a strongbox bound for Madagascar, ten thousand leagues off. When a man in Tortuga cracks his chest and finds the coin lying crown-up, the other in Madagascar shall lie cross-up. Every time, without fail.

"Bah!" says ye. "'Tis no witchery! 'Tis like a pair of boots!"

Aye, a sharp-witted objection, and I'd keelhaul any man who didn't raise it. If I pack a left boot in one sea-chest and a right in t'other, then whoever opens his chest knows straightaway what his shipmate holds. The boots were left and right all along. 'Tis plain cargo, no devilry.

But here be the black magic of it

These cursed doubloons are not like boots. Before any man lays eyes upon 'em, neither coin has chosen crown nor cross. Each lies in a fog of maybe, spinning like a coin flipped in the dark, being both and neither. Only at the moment a man throws open the lid does the fog lift. And in that very instant, the coin ten thousand leagues away settles itself contrary, quicker than a cannon's flash.

"How can ye know they hadn't settled it secret-like beforehand?" asks the quartermaster.

A fair question, and the learned gentlemen squabbled over it for many a year. Here be the test: ye don't merely open the chests. Ye inspect each coin through a spyglass held at some crooked slant, chosen at a whim, one slant in Tortuga and another in Madagascar. Do this a thousand times over, and keep careful tally in the ship's log.

When the two logbooks be laid side by side, the agreements come out too cozy. No secret plan, no hidden orders writ in the coins before they sailed, could ever produce such a tally. The numbers prove it as sure as a compass points north. The coins were truly undecided till the looking, yet bound together all the same.

"Then we can send word faster than any ship!" cries the powder monkey.

Avast, ye eager whelp! The sea is crueler than that. Each man, opening his own chest, sees naught but a random toss. Crown or cross, fair odds, no pattern. He cannot choose what his coin shows, so he cannot stamp a message upon it. The fellow in Madagascar sees only chance and knows nothing of what passed in Tortuga. Only when the two logbooks are fetched together, by honest sail and slow wind, does the uncanny match reveal itself.

So ye'll have no swifter way to warn your mates of the Navy's approach. The curse binds the coins, but it carries no letters.

The moral, me hearties

The world, at its smallest fathoms, does not behave as boots in chests. Some things be joined by bonds that care naught for leagues of open water. And the very act of looking stirs the deep.

Now. Who's drunk my rumbullion?

Translation note for landlubbers: the doubloons are entangled particles; "crown or cross" is a measured property such as spin; the "fog of maybe" is superposition; the spyglass slants and logbook tallies are Bell tests, which rule out hidden pre-arranged answers; and the powder monkey's disappointment is the no-communication theorem, which is why entanglement can't send messages faster than light.

instruction.html:
The Twinned Doubloons: A Lecture Given Below Decks

Gather 'round, ye bilge-rats, and stow yer grog. The Captain hath a tale of sorcery stranger than any kraken.

I. Of the Cursed Coins

Picture two doubloons, struck from the same cursed gold in the same unholy hour. Call 'em twinned. Now, a common coin lies heads or tails in yer purse whether ye look upon it or no. Not these devils. Until some scallywag claps eyes upon 'em, they lie neither heads nor tails, but spin betwixt the two like a drunkard who can't choose between the rum and the wench. Aye, both and neither, all at once.

II. Of the Parting

Now hark. I keep one coin in my sea-chest here at Tortuga. The other I give to One-Eyed Morgan, and he sails it a thousand leagues to the far end of the Spanish Main.

The moment Morgan opens his chest and finds his coin showing heads, mine, a thousand leagues hence, in that very instant, falls tails. Every time. Faster than a cannon shot, faster than a gull, faster than the lightning itself. No messenger, no rope, no hidden passage betwixt 'em.

III. "Bah! 'Twas Fixed from the Start!"

Ye there, Bosun, I see the doubt in yer squinting eye. Ye reckon 'tis like a pair of boots: one left, one right, shoved in two chests. Open yours and find the left boot, and of course the other's the right. No witchery in that.

A sharp thought, and wrong as a Spaniard's map.

For there be clever men who put these coins to trickier tests: looking at 'em slantwise, from this angle and that, in a hundred cunning combinations. And when they tallied the results in their ledgers, the numbers came out more agreeable than any pair of boots, or any secret plan made in port, could ever account for. The coins were not decided beforehand. Their fates were sworn together, like two men who signed the same Articles in blood. What befalls one is bound to the other, no matter the leagues between.

IV. "Then We'll Send Secret Messages, Cap'n!"

Belay that, ye greedy powder monkey. 'Tis the cruelest jest of the whole curse.

Morgan cannot choose which face his coin shows. 'Tis pure chance, a toss of the dice in Davy Jones's own hand. So when I open my chest and see tails, I've learned nothing of Morgan's doings, only that his fell heads. To know we matched, he must still send me a letter by ordinary sloop. No signal outruns the wind by this trick. The sea keeps her speed limit, even if her coins do not.

V. The Moral

So there 'tis, lads. Two coins, one fate. Spinning in doubt till looked upon, bound together across any distance, with no secret plan between 'em, and yet useless for carrying news.

The learned gentlemen call it entanglement. Even the great natural philosopher Einstein, a landlubber of a later age, cursed it as "spooky action at a distance."

I call it the only treasure in all the world that's worth nothing to steal and everything to understand.

Now back to yer posts, and if any man finds his coin spinning, report it to the quartermaster. 🏴‍☠️

plain.html:
Gather ‘round the lantern, ye bilge rats, and pin back yer good ear! I be tellin’ ye of a dark and ghostly magic that haunts the very waters we sail. The wig-wearin’ scholars on land ain’t got a name fer it, but I calls it the "Witch’s Knot."

To understand this cursed witchcraft, ye must first imagine a pair of fine, silver pieces of eight.

Now, if a regular scallywag flips a coin into the dark hold of a ship, it be either landin' on the King’s Head or the Jolly Roger. But these ain't regular coins. These be enchanted doubloons. While they be flyin’ through the black of the hold, unseen by any sailor's eye, they ain't heads, and they ain't tails. They be a ghostly, swirling mist of both at the exact same time. They only pick a side the very second ye bring yer lantern close and lay yer eye upon ‘em.

Now, here be the true madness. Suppose a sea-hag takes these two enchanted coins, spits on ‘em, and binds ‘em together with a cursed spell before tossing ‘em into the air. They be forever linked, mates. Tied by an invisible rigging that no cutlass can sever.

Ye take one of these spinnin’, misty coins and lock it in a stout wooden chest here in Port Royal. Ye give the second spinnin’ coin to yer quartermaster, lock it in his chest, and tell him to sail a thousand leagues away to the shores of Tortuga.

Both coins be miles apart, still trapped in that ghostly blur of neither heads nor tails.

But mark me words! The very heartbeat ye crack open yer chest in Port Royal and lay yer eye on yer coin—say it freezes on the King’s Head—at that exact, fleeting second, a thousand leagues away, the quartermaster’s coin stops its ghostly spinnin' and slams down on the Jolly Roger!

Did a messenger bird fly across the sea to tell the second coin what to do? Nay! Did a swift galleon carry a letter across the waves? Nay! Faster than a crack o' lightning, faster than the thought of God Himself, the second coin knew the fate of the first. Distance meant naught to the curse!

It matters not if yer mate sailed to Tortuga, or Davy Jones' Locker, or the very edge of the map where the sea serpents dwell. When ye look at one, the other obeys. They share one soul across the great, black ocean.

It be a strange, eerie sea we sail, mates. Now close yer gaping maws and fetch yer captain a pint of rum, for thinkin’ on the invisible rigging of the world has given me a fierce ache in the skull! Arrr!

instruction.html:
Gather 'round the capstan, ye bilge rats, and open yer ears. I’ll tell ye of a witchery darker than Davy Jones’ own locker. The scholars ashore call it natural philosophy, but any sailor worth his salt knows a cursed tether when he sees one.

Think on a pair of Spanish doubloons, forged from the exact same melted-down chalice in a black magic fire. These ain't regular coin. They be bound together by a phantom rigging—a knot ye can’t see, no matter how hard ye squint through yer spyglass.

Now, take one of these cursed doubloons and toss it high into the sea mist. While it be tumbling in the fog, what is it? Is it showing the King’s mug, or the Royal crest? Truth be told, until it hits the deck and ye lay yer good eye upon it, it ain’t neither, and it be both! It’s a ghost coin, spinning in the dark.

Here be the true madness of the sea. Ye put one of these twin doubloons in yer velvet pouch, and ye sail to the furthest shores of the East Indies. Ye leave the other coin in the pocket of yer quartermaster back in Port Royal, ten thousand leagues across the salt.

Ye stand in a tavern in the Indies. Ye flip yer coin. The very instant it slaps against the wet wood and ye look upon the King’s mug, the coin in Port Royal—half a world away—stops its ghostly spinning in the quartermaster's pocket. It instantly locks dead onto the Royal crest. Every single time.

No messenger parrot flew between 'em. No fast galleon carried the word. No signal fire was lit. Faster than the spark of a flintlock, the fate of one decided the fate of the other. It defies the wind, the waves, and the stars we steer by. The two coins be one soul, split across the oceans, whispering to each other in the dark.

If that don't chill yer blood and make ye fear the invisible tides of this world, then ye’ve no sense in yer skull at all. Now, pass the rum.

plain.html:
Arrr, gather ‘round, ye scurvy dogs, and let me spin ye a yarn ‘bout the strangest treasure in all the seven seas—quantum entanglement! Aye, ‘tis a ghostly dance o’ two cursed doubloons that be bound tighter than a kraken’s grip, though they be leagues apart.

Here’s how it be: Ye take two golden coins, but these ain’t no ordinary pieces o’ eight. They be bewitched—marked by the same devil’s sigil, say, a skull on one side and a crossbones on the other. Now, ye toss one coin to yer first mate on the Black Pearl sailin’ east, and the other to yer bosun on the Flying Dutchman sailin’ west. No matter how far they drift—be it a fathom or ‘cross the whole briny deep—when one coin shows skull, the other instant-like shows crossbones, as if the sea itself whispered the answer between ‘em!

But here’s the maddenin’ part, ye bilge rats: No signal passes between ‘em. Not a message in a bottle, not a carrier pigeon, not even the wind’s own breath! They just know, like two old salts who’ve shared too much grog and finish each other’s sentences. Try to peek at one coin afore the other, and the spell breaks—ye’ll find it flip-floppin’ like a drunken sailor ‘til ye look.

Aye, even the great Sir Isaac Newton himself would scratch his powdered wig at this, for it defies all reason! The coins be entangled, bound by some unseen pact o’ the cosmos, as if Davy Jones himself tied their fates together. And if ye think ye can outsmart it by changin’ one coin’s mark, the other’ll shift to match, faster than a cannonball from a Spanish galleon!

So there ye have it, lads—quantum entanglement be the devil’s own riddle, a treasure that mocks the very laws o’ the sea and sky. And if ye still don’t fathom it, well… that’s why they call it quantum!

Now, pass the rum afore me head explodes like a faulty powder keg! Yarrr!

instruction.html:
Arr matey, gather 'round and let ol' Cap'n Blackbeard spin ye a yarn 'bout the strangest dance o' the high seas—aye, the quantum entanglement, as the landlubber scholars call it.

Picture this: ye have two doubloons, shiny as the moon on a calm night. But these ain't no ordinary coins, savvy? They be bewitched, bound together by some devil’s trick o’ the deep. Now, ye take one doubloon and sail it to the farthest isle in the East, and the other to the frozen wastes o’ the North. No matter how far apart they be—be it a league or a thousand—if ye flip one and it lands heads, the other’ll instant-like land tails, as if the very sea itself whispered the news between ‘em!

Aye, ye might think, “That be witchcraft!” And ye’d not be wrong, but the sorcery ain’t in the coins—it’s in the way o’ the world. The two doubloons, though separated by storm and distance, be still one in some ghostly fashion. Change the one, and the other knows, faster than light, faster than thought, faster than the wind in a gale.

Now, the landlubbers in their fine coats call this “spooky action at a distance,” and they scratch their heads mightily over it. But to us pirates, who’ve seen the sea do things no man can fathom? Well, we just nod, take a swig o’ rum, and say, “Aye, the world be stranger than we know.”

So there ye have it, matey—two coins, one fate, bound by the devil’s own dice. And if ye ever find such doubloons yerself, best not gamble ‘em away… for the sea always collects its due.

plain.html:
Avast, ye scurvy dogs and bilge rats! Gather 'round the capstan and I'll spin ye a yarn of the strangest sorcery in all the seven seas—a curse that binds two pieces of treasure as one, though they lie leagues apart.

Suppose ye've plundered a chest from a Spanish galleon, and within ye find a gold doubloon most peculiar. Strike it with yer cutlass and cleave it clean in twain. Now send one half aboard a swift sloop bound for Tortuga, whilst ye keep the other locked in yer sea chest here upon the deck.

Now here's the devilry: though these two halves be separated by the breadth of the ocean, by storm and calm, they remain bound by a tether invisible—like the rigging that holds fast the mast, though no man can see the wind itself.

Each half lies in doubt, like a die cast spinning in the air, being neither heads nor tails but both at once, until ye lift the lid of the chest and look upon it with yer own eyes. The very moment ye spy that yer piece shows the King's head, the other half—be it in the hold of a ship, be it at the bottom of the briny deep—straightway shows tails! 'Tis done faster than a cannonball flies from the gunport, quicker than a man can cry "Avast!" No messenger passes between 'em, no rope connects 'em, yet the one knows the fashion of the other as surely as ye know yer own name.

'Tis as if the Devil himself had split one coin into two, yet kept 'em as one in his ledger. No matter how many leagues of water lie between, when ye turn one, the other turns with it—magic most foul and wondrous, proving that the smallest motes of the world are not so small at all, but are all connected by threads only Heaven can see.

instruction.html:
Avast, ye scurvy dogs! Haul yerselves to the capstan and I'll spin ye a yarn about the strangest sorcery in all of Nature...

Take a doubloon of Spanish gold and cleave it clean in twain with yer cutlass. Send one half to Tortuga, keep the other in yer pouch here at Port Royal. Now mark this well: afore ye lay eyes upon yer piece, it is neither King's head nor tail, but spinning in the air like a coin tossed by the Devil himself. Yet the very instant ye catch it and see the King's face staring up, ye know—aye, swifter than shot from a twelve-pounder—that the half in Tortuga shows the tail, though no messenger could cross that brine in the time it takes a cannonball to fly!

So it is with the tiniest corpuscles of matter, born together in one fiery blast like two shot cast from the same mold. Part them asunder, and they remain bound by a cable no mortal eye can see, stretching clear across the seven seas and beyond. Whirl one widdershins, and its twin—though it rest in the hold of a galleon bound for the East Indies—whirls sunwise in that same heartbeat! Until ye fix yer gaze upon 'em, each spins both ways at once, neither one nor t'other, like a weathercock in a tempest. No signal passes 'twixt them—no rope, no sail, no smoke—yet they move as one flesh, as though the sea itself whispers the secret from one to the other.

'Tis magic most foul, making a mockery of distance and time, matey!

plain.html:
Arrr, gather ‘round, ye scurvy dogs, and lend me thine ears, for I shall spin ye a tale o’ two cursed dice—aye, not the kind ye roll in taverns, but ghostly dice, flung to t’opposite ends o’ the seven seas!

Now, imagine ye cast one die upon the deck o’ the Flying Mackerel, and ‘tis rolled a six—six pips as clear as Davy Jones’ beard. Now, mark me well: its cursed twin, though banished to the far side o’ the world, say, upon a desert isle where Blackbeard’s ghost paces, shall roll a one—not by chance, but by some dark, invisible thread that binds ‘em tight!

These dice, ye see, be not rollin’ till ye look upon ‘em. Nay! They be in a foggy limbo, neither six nor one, till a bold soul dares peek. But the moment ye spy one, the other knows—aye, faster than a cutlass flash—and becomes its fated match, though no message be sent, no raven flown, no signal fired.

‘Tis called entanglement, this witchery! Two things, once touched, stay linked across leagues and leagues, defying the natural order. No wind, no current, no powder trail connects ‘em, yet they act as one soul in two bodies.

The land-lubbers in wigs and wenchless towers call it “quantum entanglement,” but we of the sea? We know ‘tis the devil’s dice, bound by a curse no compass can chart. And though Newton’s laws be strong, even he could not explain this spectral dance.

So beware, ye bold mariners: the world be stranger than the briny deep, and some bonds be not forged in iron, but in the very fabric o’ fate itself!

Now, who’s fer grog? This be enough mind-play for one eve!

instruction.html:
Arrr, gather ‘round, ye swabs and scallywags, and lend me th’ one good ear—aye, the one not chewed off by a kraken—while I spin ye a tale o’ two cursed dice, forged in the belly o’ Davy Jones his ownself!

Now, imagine ye be a scurvy dog like meself, sailin’ th’ Seven Seas, and ye come upon a pair o’ enchanted dice, blessed—or cursed—by a vengeful sea witch. Ye take one die to yer ship, and a rival sea-dog takes th’ other, and ye sail to opposite ends o’ the world—ye to the Indies, he to the icy north where even the rum freezes.

Here be the queer part: each die, when thrown, shows a number at random—1 to 6, like any honest(ish) die. But every time—every single cursed time—whenever yer rival rolls his die and gets a three, yours shows three too, even if ye not even lookin’! And if he rolls a six, so do ye, no matter the distance, no matter the storm, no matter how many bottles o’ grog ye’ve spilled on the chart.

They’re bound, see? Not by rope nor chain, but by some deep magic woven in the very sails o’ fate. Ye can’t use ‘em to send messages—like “beware the siren’s song” or “the captain’s gone mad again”—but the dice know each other’s roll, instant-like, faster than a cutlass flash.

The wise men o’ the Royal Society, in their wigs and quills, call this spooky action at a distance, and they pull out what hair they’ve left tryin’ to make sense o’ it. But we, we be men o’ the sea—we don’t need no sense! We know the world be queerer than a mermaid’s dream.

So that, me hearties, is entanglement: two things, once touched, forever bound, no matter how far the tides tear ‘em apart. Like a love between a pirate and his first ship—lost, but never broken.

Now, who’s fer rum? And keep yer hands off me die—them be cursed, and I’ve seen men go mad just starin’ at ‘em too long!

plain.html: Arr, lend an ear! Take two white stones, and bind them with a curse and the black wind. One goes west, one goes east, far beyond any bell or horn. If a hand takes the west stone and sees a red mark, the east stone will show a blue mark in that same breath. No ship nor bird can carry word, and yet the stones agree. But mark ye, no man can choose the mark, nor send word through the bond. It is fate alone; the secret stays with the sea, though leagues stand between the stones.

instruction.html: Hark ye, shipmate. Take two doubloons, turned in one dark hold, and tied by a thread no eye can see. Before ye look, no face is sure; the dark holds the turn. Set one in a chest on this ship, the other in a chest on a ship yonder. Draw the first: if the king’s face looks up, the other, how far off soever, must show the lion. No hand, rope, gull, or word carried by wind can tell the far coin to show another face. The two were one fate, split in twain, and the split still wears one seal. Ye cannot use that thread to send tidings; it only reveals what was bound ere the coins were parted. So mark ye: the deep keeps a knot no eye can find. Two coins far apart, yet one fate beating in both.

plain.html:
On the Curious Business of Entangled Doubloons

Gather 'round, ye scurvy sea dogs, and lend an ear to the strangest tale ever sailed out of the natural philosophy trade!

Imagine, if ye will, that ye and yer trusty first mate each pocket a coin from the same cursed treasure chest — coins what were forged together by some witchy smithery down in the depths. Ye know not which faces they bear, mind ye — heads or tails, they be a mystery wrapped in fog.

Now here be the devil's own trick, and I swear it on Davy Jones' locker itself: ye sail one way 'cross the briny deep, and yer mate sails the other way, farther apart than the Crown's navy could ever spy. Ye might be a thousand leagues asunder — ye in some godforsaken cove, yer mate frozen stiff near the pole itself!

But the moment ye flip yer coin and peer upon it — by the powers, the very instant ye lay eyes on it — yer mate's coin reveals itself too, as if it heard whispered news upon a wind that blows faster than any ship or cannonball could ever ride!

And here's the true black magic of it: if yer coin shows heads, his shows tails. Always. No matter the distance. No matter that no raven, no message in a bottle, no signal fire passed between ye. 'Tis as though the coins be not two coins at all, but one fate wearing two faces!

Some learned landlubber wizards — they call themselves "physicists" now, fancy that — claim no treasure map can explain this, for the coins weren't secretly agreed upon their faces beforehand. Nay, they say the coins had no faces at all until someone looked! The very act of spyin' upon one doth conjure the other's fortune, instant-like, 'cross any ocean ye please.

Old Einstein himself — a right clever sea dog of the chalkboards — grumbled that this be "spooky action at a distance," like a ghost rattlin' chains from port to starboard across the whole world. He reckoned there must be some hidden chart, some secret coordinates we scoundrels hadn't found yet. But those whelps with their fancy experiments have tested it a hundred times over, and blast me eyes, the spooky wind be real!

Now don't ye go thinkin' ye can use these coins to send messages across the sea, mind ye — the fortune be random as a storm, and no scallywag can pick what face appears. Ye'll see the mystery only when ye and yer mate sail home and compare yer plunder, side by side.

But mark me words: this entangled booty be the very heart of a new kind of sorcery — machines what cipher messages no pirate nor king can crack, and contraptions what reckon more sums than there be stars in the sky.

So hoist the colors, ye scallywags — the universe itself be dealin' from a deck where two cards be one hand, no matter how far ye sail 'em apart!

Now someone fetch me rum. All this philosophy's made me parched. 🏴‍☠️

instruction.html:
Quantum Entanglement, As Explained by Captain Redbeard Q. Skeffington, Upon the Quarterdeck

Gather round, ye scurvy sea-dogs, and lend an ear, for I shall tell ye of the strangest magick ever to vex a natural philosopher — stranger than the kraken, stranger than the ghost light what follows a doomed ship through fog.

Now, ye know how a doubloon be cut clean in twain? Take ye such a coin, snap it asunder, and give one half to yer brother pirate in Tortuga whilst ye keep the other in yer own coat. Ye sail the seven seas, far apart — him in the Caribbee, ye round the Cape of Good Hope. Yet here be the marvel: the instant ye look upon yer half and see it be the heads half, ye know — faster than a cannonball, faster than gossip in a rum house — that yer brother holds the tails half. No letter need be sent. No pigeon loosed. The knowledge simply be.

"But Captain," pipes up young Fletcher, ever the doubting bilge rat, "that be no magick at all! 'Tis like two gloves — ye keep the left, yer mate must have the right!"

Aye, clever lad — and for many a year, the learned ashore men said the very same. They said: "The coin were fated from the moment it were snapped. Some secret mark, some hidden ink upon the doubloon, decided it all beforehand. Nothing spooky about it!"

But here be where the sea turns truly uncanny, me hearties. These particles of light — call 'em "glints," if ye like — be not like doubloons nor gloves. Take two glints what have been tangled together (the natural philosophers say "entangled," and who am I to argue with men in powdered wigs), and send one to Tortuga and one to the Cape. Then look upon one of them — and here's the devil of it — it hath no fixed nature until ye look. 'Tis neither heads nor tails nor port nor starboard, but a fog of maybe, a sea of "could be anything." And the very moment ye spy it and it settles into one shape, its far-off twin also settles — into the opposite shape, always, every time, like a curse written into the very bones of creation.

And mark this well: no smuggler's note passes between them. No ship, no whisper, no smoke signal. Nothing travels the distance between 'em. Yet they know of each other instant, as if the space between be no space at all — as if the two glints, however far sundered, remain one single soul wearing two coats.

Old Einstein hisself — a wise man, though he wore no proper beard nor knew the feel of a rope — called it "spooky action at a distance," and grumbled that God must not play at dice. But the sea don't care what ye grumble about, and neither do the glints. The learned men ran their trials — clever trials, sharper than any cutlass — and found the hidden-mark theory wanting. The universe, it seems, truly doth decide its business only when observed, and binds its far-flung kin together in ways no chart can show.

Can ye use it to send word to yer brother faster than wind? Nay, ye lubber, and don't be daft — each look shows ye a random face, and randomness carries no message, like a parrot what squawks gibberish. But bind two glints together and they stay bound — and scoundrels ashore be already scheming to build unbreakable codes and strange new engines upon this very sorcery.

So there ye have it: two souls, one fate, no message between, and the whole thing proven true by men who've never once spliced a mainbrace.

Now someone fetch the rum, for I've earned it, and physics be thirsty work.

plain.html:
Arrr, gather round, ye scurvy dogs, and I'll spin ye a tale of the queerest magic what sails the seven seas of creation — the cursed bond they call quantum entanglement.

Now, ye know how it goes with ordinary cargo. Ye load a chest of gold in Tortuga, and ye sail it to Port Royal. The gold and the ship each go their own way, aye? The chest don't give a hang where the ship be, nor the ship for the chest. Separate as two drunken sailors in different taverns.

But here's the devil's own trick. Imagine two wee coins — call 'em the Twinned Doubloons — forged together in a fire so strange that they share one soul between 'em. Ye snatch one up and stuff it in yer pocket, and yer mate takes t'other to the far side of the world, past the Cape of Good Hope and beyond. Now ye flip yer doubloon. 'Tis heads, says ye.

And in that very instant — faster than a gull can blink, faster than any cannonball flies — yer mate's doubloon, half a world away, knows it must show tails. Not because ye sent a message by pigeon or signal lamp. Nay! There be no message at all. The two coins was forged as one cursed thing, and what one does, t'other answers, though an ocean and a hundred years of sailing lie between 'em.

And here's the part what makes the learned men weep into their grog: till ye flip yer coin, neither doubloon be heads nor tails at all. They be both at once — a ghostly haze of heads-and-tails, like a fog bank what ain't decided which way to blow. Only when ye clap eyes on yer coin does the fog lift and the answer fix itself — and in that same breath, yer mate's coin is fixed too.

But mark me well, ye lubbers — ye can't use this to send word! Ye can't choose heads or tails; the coin decides, not ye. So ye can't spell out "SAVE ME" to yer mate across the sea. All ye get is the certainty that whatever ye see, he'll see the opposite. 'Tis a bond for knowin', not for tellin'. Many a clever captain has tried to make a signal of it and ended up talking to the fishes.

And the wise men o' the Royal Society, they argue yet about how the two coins conspire — whether some secret wind carries the word invisible, or whether the world be stranger than that and the coins truly be one thing wearing two coats. That debate'll rage till the seas boil dry, I reckon.

So there 'tis: two doubloons, one soul, no message, and a certainty that binds 'em across all the waters of the world. Now pass the rum, and don't ye be askin' me to explain it twice — me head's already spinnin' like a compass in a storm.

instruction.html:
Arrr, gather round, ye scurvy dogs, and I'll spin ye a tale of the strangest treasure in all creation—what the learned men call quantum entanglement.

Now listen close. Imagine ye take two doubloons from the same cursed hoard, and ye polish 'em so they're twins o' the same mint. Then ye stow one in yer pocket and give t'other to yer mate aboard a ship bound for the far side o' the world—aye, past the Indies, past where the maps say "here be dragons."

Here's the devilry: these two coins ain't merely alike. They're bound—joined by a hex no witch nor sea-ghost could sever. Flip yer doubloon and it shows heads. At that very instant—not a heartbeat later, not the time it takes a gull to blink—yer mate's coin, leagues and leagues away, shows tails. And 'twas never decided which coin would show what till the very moment o' the flipping! The coins had no secret plan betwixt 'em. The answer was written in the act o' the asking, and both coins answered as one.

Ye'll say, "Cap'n, surely some messenger slipped through the rigging and told the other coin." But nay! No messenger. No signal. No whisper on the wind. The sea herself couldn't carry word that fast—not even light, the swiftest thing in all creation, could make that voyage in time. The coins are simply one thing wearing two faces, like a man with a foot on each o' two ships. Ask the one, and the other answers.

And here's the cruel jest that makes philosophers weep into their grog: ye cannot use this hex to send a message. Try to force the coin to show heads as ye please, and the spell shatters—the bond dissolves like fog at dawn. The coins only keep their promise when ye let the flipping fall as it may.

So there ye have it. Two coins, one fate, no rope between 'em, and no word can pass. 'Tis the deepest magic in the whole o' the deep—and 'twas never a pirate's trick at all, but the way o' the world herself, stranger than any kraken or ghost ship. Now pass the rum, and dinna ask me to explain it twice.

plain.html:
Avast there, ye scurvy bilge rat! Grab a tankard o' grog and lend an ear, fer I be tellin' ye the tale of the most haunted plunder in all the seven seas — they calls 'em the Entangled Doubloons.

Picture it, matey. A one-eyed sorcerer hands me and my first-mate two golden doubloons, one apiece. Then he splits us clean across the world: I sail to the Isle o' Spices, and the scallywag sets course fer Davy Jones' Locker 'erself — light-years away by the swiftest galleon.

Now here be the witchcraft. Before either o' us looks, that doubloon ain't heads nor tails — it be both at once, spinin' in the air like a question scrawled in sea-foam. It don't decide nothin' till a hungry eye falls upon it.

Then comes the curse. The very instant I flip me coin and watch it land on heads, my mate's coin — clear across the world, past every reef and horizon — settles straightway to tails. No bell tolled, no raven flew the message, nothin'. It just knows. Flip me piece o' eight a thousand times, and hers will always be the opposite, quicker than any canon-ball could cross the water.

"Hold on," ye say, scratchin' yer pegleg. "Ain't that like tearin' a pair o' gloves in two and shipmin' 'em in locked chests? Open yer chest, see a left glove, and ye know theirs be right?" Aye, that'd be senseable. But no, ye barnacle — these doubloons weren't neither heads nor tails to begin with! They were truly undecided, both o' 'em, right till the moment the eyes fell upon 'em. The sorcerer fooled even himself. When I peek and mine chooses tails, it be choosin' as likely as a coin toss — and hers obeys in the same breath.

So can a clever captain use this to fire a secret signal across the ocean? Blimey, no. Fer me result be as random as the wind in the sails — I can't make me coin come up heads to spell out "send more rum." My mate just sees her coin dance to whatever fortune dealt us. Neither o' us commands the treasure; we only ever find our coins agreed, long after the fact.

That be the haunted plunder of it, savvy? Two bits o' sea-magic, bound soul-to-soul across every league o' blue, answerin' to one another the moment ye dare to look — yet tellin' no secret and carryin' no message, just like a pair o' lovers separated by the sea who somehow always weep on the very same day.

Arr. Now that's what they teach at the ol' academy.

instruction.html:
Ah, gather 'round, ye scurvy lot, an' I'll tell ye o' the strangest trick the Sea ever played, though 'tis no trick at all—'tis what them powdered natural philosophers be squabblin' over in their towers o' learning.

Listen sharp.

Say ye have two specks o' matter, smaller than a grain o' sand off Tortuga, so wee ye can't spy 'em with the keenest glass at the topmost mast. Now, these two bit'rs get caught up in the same mischief—took the same cannonade, dragged through the same murky water together—so that they come to share a single fate, like two deckhands tied fast to one rope. We call this bond entangle. Their fortunes be knotted as one.

Here be the witchery of it: whilst no eye gazes upon 'em, neither o' the two specks has made up its mind which way to spin—port or starboard. It be both and neither at once, a fog o' maybes hangin' in the bilge water, until somebody comes an' takes a look-see. That glance be like the cap'n's whistle—it settles the whole dang crew right smart.

Now here be where me belly turns over: ye take one a' these fickle specks an' haul it clear to the Spanish Main, an' leave the other anchored off some lonely isle half the world away. Look at the one in yer palm and—there she settles, spins starboard, say. And mark me words, that other bit o' mischief, clear across the drowned horizon, will settle on port the very same instant. No time passes between 'em. Not a beat. Not a tick of the ship's glass.

'Ere be the part that gives old Captain Einstein the vapours—"spooky action at a distance," he grumbles through his pipe. Them two far-flung rogues feel each other without signal fire, without parrot or messenger, without a single rowboat between 'em. They simply know, like a pair o' twins separated at sea who both catch the ache in their chest on a certain tide.

But hold—the treasure be buried, yet there be no shortcut to plunder it quick-like. Ye can't make yer speck choose starboard when ye please; the roll of the dice be fair and fickle still. So though they answer each other faster than thought, ye landlubbers can't smuggle a secret note through 'em, nor shout a warning to a friend clean across the world. The riddle holds its tongue. All ye know till ye look be a coin spinna in the dark, an' when ye at last peek—well, ye'll find out what the other scoundrel's doin' same as you, that's all the spoils ye get.

So there it is, mates: two thieves bound by one rope of fate, scattered to the four winds, yet swingin' together when at last the lantern's lit. The Sea herself couldn't tie a knot so curious.

Now hand o'er the rum afore me head spins faster than them wee scallywags.

plain.html:
Yeah, I totally get that.

That silence just screams “something’s off,” even if your brain hasn’t quite figured out what yet.

It’s not about knowing exactly what’s behind it — it’s about trusting that your gut’s picking up on something you haven’t seen clearly yet.

And when you notice it, even if it’s just a faint feeling, you’ve already got a head start. That’s self-awareness, and it’s a huge advantage.

So yeah, trust that instinct. It’s like your internal radar, and it’s tuned way sharper than people give it credit for.

instruction.html:
Listen close, mate. Imagine two cursed coins, minted from the same cursed gold. One’s in your hand; the other’s at the bottom of the ocean. When you flip yours and it lands heads, the other one—miles away—instantly lands tails. No delay, no message flying between them. Just… done.

That’s entanglement, in the King’s English. Two particles once joined are forever linked, no matter the distance. Flip one, and its partner reacts like it’s watching. It’s not magic—it’s just the way reality’s built.

Like the sea and the moon, mate. Separate, but always in sync.

plain.html:
Let’s talk about “quantum entanglement” using only 17th-century pirate-speak.

Aboard the ship, we’ve got two crew members—let’s call them Redbeard and Blackbeard. Each sailor has their own locked chest filled with gold coins. Both chests are identical in every way—they’re made of the same wood, weigh the same, and are nailed shut with ten rusty nails.

Here’s where things get tricky: the chests are placed at opposite ends of the ship—one at the bow, one at the stern—and then Redbeard sets fire to the ship. The flaming vessel sails over a treacherous waterfall and explodes in a massive fireball at the bottom.

Now—here’s where it gets weird. Miraculously, Blackbeard survives by jumping overboard just before the explosion. He washes up on an island on the other side of the waterfall, holding only one chest—his own. Redbeard, however, is nowhere to be seen—he’s presumed lost at sea.

Here’s the twist: when Blackbeard opens his chest, it’s full of redbeard’s gold—not his own. The chests have switched contents! But here’s the kicker: Blackbeard’s missing pinky finger, which was famously lopped off in a drunken duel with Redbeard weeks ago.

What happened?

Scientific Explanation:
The chests represent entangled quantum particles—specifically spin-half particles such as electrons or photons. Each chest is in a “superposition” state, with equal probability of containing either set of gold coins.

When Blackbeard jumped off the ship (measuring which chest he grabbed), the act of observation caused his chest to collapse into one specific state—containing Redbeard’s gold. That collapse “quantum-measurement” across the waterfall instantaneously causes Redbeard’s chest to also collapse—even though Redbeard himself isn’t around to observe it.

Pirate-Speak Summary:
Blackbeard jumped overboard and grabbed one chest—his act of observation caused his chest to become “possessed” by Redbeard’s gold. The missing pinky finger represents a quantum-measurement interaction where Blackbeard himself is no longer in his original “state.”

Redbeard remains lost at sea because his chest collapsed into containing Blackbeard’s gold—but Blackbeard himself is now “quantum-entangled” with Redbeard’s missing finger.

Final Question: If Blackbeard ever finds Redbeard alive on a desert island—but never tells Redbeard about the switch—does Redbeard ever notice his “own” chest is full of Blackbeard’s gold? Why or why not?

instruction.html:
Ah, you’ve chosen a challenge worthy of a scurvy sea dog like me.

Entanglement—well, that’s when two particles are bound together in such a way that they’re no longer two separate things but one interconnected thing. Doesn’t matter how far apart they are—one changes, the other does too, instantly. Some scientists say this means time and distance don’t work the way we think they do. Others call it “spooky action at a distance” because it’s hard to wrap your head around.

In pirate terms? Imagine two compass needles—identical twins born from the same ship’s compass. No matter where you take them in the world, if you spin one, the other spins too, even across oceans. Now imagine this happening instantly—faster than even light could travel across those oceans.

The strangest part? If you measure one needle carefully, the other needle—even if you’ve never touched it—suddenly changes in a way that matches exactly what you’ve done to the first.

It defies all sense but there’s mountains of experimental evidence backing it up.

Honestly? Makes you question whether distance itself is real or just something our brains tell us for convenience.

plain.html:
If two coins are linked by fate, and you toss one on a merchant ship in the fog, then the other coin back in Bristol always lands the same way — not because they share a string, but because the sea itself whispers between them.

This is called entanglement. You don't need to be near it for the whisper to arrive, which has confounded physicists since the Enlightenment. The ancient pirates understood it as "doom paired with its shadow."

instruction.html:
Aye, that’s a challenge. All right, then.

“Quantum entanglement,” you say? Well, here’s the pirate version. Imagine two buccaneers standing at opposite ends of a battlefield, each with a loaded pistol aimed straight at the other. Now, before they fire, a wizard walks between them, waves his wand, and says, “Here’s the trick: whichever of you pulls the trigger first, the bullet flies to both your hearts at once.”

That’s entanglement in a nutshell.

Now, here’s the twist — the wizard doesn’t actually fire either gun. He just enchants them so that whatever happens to one, the same thing instantly happens to the other, no matter how far apart they are. If the buccaneer on the left fires, his counterpart falls dead across the battlefield, and vice versa.

Here’s the strange part: if you put those pistols miles apart — on separate islands, even — and one of them is fired, the man on the distant island still collapses dead before the news has time to row between them. No message, no signal, no pigeon with a note tied to its leg. Just: boom, he’s down.

And here’s the real kicker: if you captured the wizard and made him explain it, he’d look at you like you were simple for asking. “Magic, obviously,” he’d say, and vanish in a puff of smoke. But the pistols would still be enchanted, still killing each other from halfway across the ocean.

That’s the beauty of it, though — even magic obeys rules we don’t understand until somebody figures them out, and once you know them, the wizard’s tricks look less magical and more predictable. That’s how science wins every time.

plain.html:
Arr, matey! Gather 'round and let me be tellin' ye a tale of the most perplexin' phenomenon in the whole wide sea—quantum entanglement, ye might call it the "Curse o' the Linked Souls."

Imagine ye two doubloons, bein' separated by the vast ocean. One doubloon ye toss to the port side, and the other to the starboard. Now, in the world o' quantum, these doubloons be linked so tight, like the heartstrings o' true love, that no matter how far ye fling 'em—be it to opposite ends o' the earth or beyond the reach o' cannonballs—their sides always match. If one flips to show the king, the other flips too, as if by magic. And not just once, but every time, without a rope or signal 'twixt them.

Some say it's the devil's work, but the wise minds o' the Enlightenment be callin' it entanglement. Two particles be born together, and though the sea may part 'em, their fates remain entwined, defying distance and all reason.

So ye see, lads and lasses, quantum entanglement be like havin' a twin on the other side o' the world—who knows your every move, even before ye make it. And no codebreaker or ship's compass can explain why. It's the greatest mystery the sea—or science—has ever seen.

instruction.html:
Arr, matey! Ye be askin' fer a tale o' the most perplexin' sort—quantum entanglement, ye say? Now, gather 'round, for I be tellin' ye a story 'bout particles, as if they be spirits of the sea, linked fer eternity, no matter how far they be scattered across the ocean.

Imagine ye two doubloons, forged in the same fire, separated by the breadth o' the seven seas. One be sent east, one west. No matter the distance, they remain as one in spirit. If one be flipped, its twin be flipped as well, even though naught be touchin' 'em—no ship, no cable, nothin'. 'Tis as if they be whisperin' across the void, faster than any wind or cannonball.

Now, in the world o' tiny things—smaller than ye can imagine—particles do the same. They be entangled, bound by a curse or blessing from the sea itself. Break the link of one, and the other be affected, even if they be on opposite sides o' the Earth. Scientists be scratchin' their heads, tryin' to figure out how it be possible. But to us, it be as simple as knowin' that what be separated cannot truly be sundered.

So, ye see, quantum entanglement be like the eternal bond o' two pirates, separated by the world, but still as one in the heart o' the sea. Arrr!

plain.html:
Ye be wantin' me to explain them fancy "quantum entanglements" like a swashbucklin' sea dog, eh? Alright then, listen close and I'll tell ye of the sea of the tiny, where particles be as sneaky as a mermaid in the dark.

Imagine two wee pearls, each one locked to its mate like a ship and its anchor. If ye toss one pearl into the sea and the other pearl starts wobblin' like a drunken sailor, don't ye go thinkin' it's just chance, matey! It's like magic, but not the sort ye find in a witch's brew. It's like... it's like the ocean itself be talkin' to them pearls, tellin' 'em to move in sync like sea siren's call.

Now, when ye separate those pearls far across the seven seas and then toss one more, that other one'll still react like it's gettin' the tides from the first, even if it be on the other side of the world. It's like they be linked by an invisible rope, one that lets 'em hear each other's whispers beneath the waves. That's the sea of quantum, where things can be connected in ways that defy the wind and the tides.

So that be quantum entanglement, me hearty — a sea of secrets, where the tiny be as bound as a ship to its anchor, and where magic be real, but only if ye be lookin' at the world with the eyes of the sea. Arrr.

instruction.html: Lad, imagine yer at sea on a dark night, sailin' in a tiny boat. Yer not sure where yer goin', but ye feel it. Every wave, every wind, seems to know the route ahead, even though ye can't see it. Now, take two boats—sisters, ye might call 'em—sailin' apart on the horizon. The wind in each one's sails is like a whisper from the mateys who stay back in the tavern. If one boat hits a rock, the other one feels it, even if they're miles apart, like a punch in the gut. That's not just the ocean talkin'; that's the spirits of the sea. It's like yer heart knows what's happenin' in yer mate's heart, even if ye can't see the other ship. That's entanglement, lad—like two pieces of a treasure map, connected across the waves, even when ye're far apart. Ye feel it, but ye don't know how. It just is.

plain.html:
Arrr, ye landlubbers! Ye be wantin' to know o' them mystic bondages o' the tiny, eh? Alright then, matey, listen close and I'll tell ye o' entwinement o' the wee particles.

Y'see, when two specks o' matter—like tiny barnacles on a sunken ship—be born together in the great ocean o' existence, they form a tie that binds 'em tighter than a trusty cutlass to yer hip. This tie, me hearty, be stronger than the fiercest sea storm, and it don't matter a whit how far ye sail 'em apart. Ye could hide one in the depths o' Davey Jones' locker and the other on the highest mast o' the Black Swan, and still, they'd be connected like two shipmates in battle.

Here be how it works, me mate: if ye do somethin' to one o' these tiny scallywags—like makin' it spin like a ship in a whirlpool—the other will start spinning too, instantly, no matter the distance between 'em. Not a single message in a bottle could sail that fast, savvy? It be like they're talkin' to each other in a secret code, faster than the wind or the waves.

Now, ye might be thinkin', "But how? What sea witchery be this?" And I'll tell ye, matey—it be the mystic sea o' probability. Ye see, sometimes these tiny particles be in many places at once, like a ghost ship on a foggy night. And when ye measure one, ye force it to decide where it wants to be, like makin' a ship drop anchor. But its entwined mate, wherever it be, will make the same decision, like two ships sailin' in formation—without a single signal flag.

So hoist the colors, me hearties, and remember: in the grand ocean o' the universe, sometimes the smallest things be bound together by the strongest o' unseen ties.

instruction.html:
Arrr, listen close me hearties, to a tale o' mysteries deep as the darkest sea. Ye see, in the vast and mystic void, tiny sparks o' matter be linked—like ships bound by an unseen chain. They be "entwined," aye, even when separated by leagues o' empty space. If one spark dances a jig, the other spark dances the same jig, instant-like—even if 'twere on the other side o' the seven seas.

They be connected by a hidden thread, a "quantum tide" that flows between 'em, faster than any galleon or cannonball. It be as if the very fabric o' reality were woven with magic, where the state o' one spark be instantly mirrored in the state o' the other—no matter the distance 'twixt them.

Think o' two lanterns on separate islands. If ye blow out the flame o' one, the other goes dark too—straight away, without a messenger or signal. That be the strange power o' "entanglement," me hearties—a mystic bond that defies time and space itself. Now, keep this under yer tricorn, or the landlubbers will think ye've gone barnacle-brained. But ye know the truth: the universe be full o' wonders stranger than sea serpents or hidden treasure.

plain.html:
Harken close, ye salt-stained scallywags, and listen to a tale of the spooky spirits of the deep. I’ll be tellin’ ye of the Curse of the Twin-Bound Doubloons—what the fancy wig-wearers call “Quantum Entanglement.”

Now, imagine two golden coins, forged in the same molten pot of a witch’s forge. These ain’t no ordinary booty. They be linked. Not by chain, nor by rope, nor by a captain’s promise. They be bound by a ghost-thread that spans the whole Seven Seas.

Ye take one coin, wrap it in a velvet pouch, and sail it to the far shores of the East Indies. Ye keep the other right here, tucked in yer tricorn hat.

Now, here be the madness: neither coin knows its own face.

They ain’t heads. They ain’t tails. They’re both… and neither. They’re shimmering in the middle, spinning like a drunken bosun in a gale. This be what the scholars call superposition, though we calls it “The Fog of Uncertainty.”

But the moment ye flip that coin in yer hat—the very instant ye look at it—the ghost-thread snaps tight.

If yer coin lands Heads, then bang! That other coin halfway ‘round the world, without a second’s delay, flips itself to Tails.

It don’t matter if there’s a thousand leagues of black water between ‘em.
It don’t matter if they’re locked in iron chests.
The instant one turns, the other knows.

Even the Great Admiral Einstein—a man with hair like a startled sea anemone—called it “spooky action at a distance.” He didn’t like it. He thought it smelled like a siren’s lie.

But the truth be this, ye scurvy dogs: the universe ain’t a clockwork map. It’s a ghostly tangle. Two things can be one soul, split across the ocean, whispering secrets faster than a cannonball’s flight.

Now… pass the rum.

instruction.html:
Gather ’round, ye salt-stained scoundrels, and harken close, for I’ll tell ye of a queer kind o’ magic... a devil’s knot tied in the very fabric o’ the deep.

Now, picture two souls—two identical cutlasses, forged in the same hellfire, tempered in the same brine. They’re entangled, see? Linked like two cursed coins tossed from a dying man’s pocket.

Ye take one blade and hoist it aboard a brigantine bound for the TORTUGAS. Ye take the other, and ye sail it ‘round the Horn to the far edge o’ the frozen east.

Now, here be the trick:

Until ye look ‘em in the eye, neither blade is true. Each one is both sharp and dull—both pointed and blunt—shimmering in a ghost-mist of maybes.

But the moment ye draw that blade in Tortugas and feel its edge... BAM!

At that very same heartbeat, halfway ‘round the world, the other blade knows.

If the first be sharp, the second instantly turns dull. If the first be blunt, the other snaps to a razor’s edge.

No messenger bird flies between ‘em. No signal flare. No whispered word through the spray. They just be. They’re tied by a phantom rope that don’t care for leagues nor oceans nor the gods themselves.

Even the Great Captain Einstein called it “spooky action at a distance.” And believe me, he looked like a man who’d seen a ghost in the hold.

So there ye have it, ye scallywags. The world ain’t just wind and tide. Sometimes, two things be one thing, even when they’re a whole world apart.

Now pass the rum before I throw the lot of ye overboard.
